texts.0: SP, due to prolonged head-down time on the GPS control panel, interrupted the instrument and outside crosscheck and did not hold the briefed navigation altitude. The excursion exceeded 300 feet and continued to develop unnoticed while data entry went on. The IP had to direct the return to the assigned altitude before the next turning point.
texts.1: SP, due to task saturation while sequencing the GPS flight plan, released altitude control and allowed the aircraft to settle. The deviation reached about 300 feet and stabilized only at the limit of tolerance. Recovery followed repeated verbal prompting from the IP rather than SP's own crosscheck.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow scan pattern while selecting GPS pages, allowed the navigation altitude to drift between 150 and 300 feet. SP detected the trend on the altimeter and returned to the briefed altitude in good time without IP input. The excursion was contained, although the pitch correction was larger than required.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation altitude within 150 feet throughout GPS programming and monitoring. Head-down periods were kept short and each one was closed with an immediate altimeter check. Corrections were small, prompt and made with smooth pitch and power inputs.
texts.4: SP held the briefed navigation altitude with negligible deviation while working the GPS. Altimeter checks were interleaved with every page selection, so no drift was allowed to build. Aircraft control remained precise and entirely unaffected by the equipment workload.
texts.marginal: SP remained within altitude standards, but every GPS entry produced a repeatable sag of about 100 feet that was corrected only after several seconds. The trend was consistent and grew with the length of the head-down period. SP is expected to shorten the interruption of the altimeter crosscheck so that altitude holding does not depend on the GPS workload.

texts.0: SP, due to inattention to power setting while entering GPS waypoint data, did not maintain the briefed navigation airspeed. The excursion passed 20 knots and left the aircraft off the planned timing to the next turning point. The IP had to call for the power correction to restore the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to reset power after a GPS-driven turn, allowed the airspeed to decay to the 20 knot limit. The value settled at the edge of tolerance and was corrected only after direct verbal cueing. SP's own crosscheck did not capture the error.
texts.2: SP, due to delayed power adjustment during GPS page management, allowed airspeed to vary between 10 and 20 knots from the briefed figure. SP identified the deviation and restored the target speed without IP intervention. Timing to the next turning point was preserved.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within 10 knots while operating the GPS. Power was set and trimmed before each head-down task, so the speed stayed stable. Ground speed and estimated times to the turning points remained consistent with the plan.
texts.4: SP held the briefed navigation airspeed with negligible variation across the whole GPS workload. Power management was anticipatory, with adjustments made before the speed could move. Timing accuracy at each turning point matched the flight plan exactly.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside airspeed standards but consistently ran near the low end of the tolerance while head-down on the GPS. Each correction was late and required a noticeable power increase. SP is expected to set and verify power before starting any GPS entry so that airspeed control stops trailing the equipment task.

error_modes.label: Heading and course tracking to the active waypoint

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated inputs while reading the GPS course window, did not fly the computed course to the active waypoint. Heading error exceeded 10 degrees and the track offset kept increasing toward the turning point. The IP had to take corrective action to regain the planned route.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the GPS course deviation indicator instead of flying a steady heading, oscillated on either side of the computed course and reached the 10 degree limit. The heading was stabilized only after IP prompting. Cross-track error at the turning point was clearly visible.
texts.2: SP, due to a late response to a small drift, allowed heading error to grow to between 5 and 10 degrees from the computed course. SP recognized the divergence on the HSI and re-established the course promptly without IP input. The turning point was still made on the planned track.
texts.3: SP flew the GPS computed course within 5 degrees on every leg. Heading corrections were small, coordinated and applied as soon as the course deviation moved. Each turning point was crossed on the planned track.
texts.4: SP tracked the GPS computed course with negligible heading error throughout the route. Drift corrections were anticipated rather than reactive, so the deviation indicator stayed centered. Turning point crossings required no late corrections.
texts.marginal: SP held heading within standards, but corrections to the computed course were repeatedly made as a series of small overshoots rather than a single input. The pattern appeared on every leg and cost track accuracy near the turning points. SP is expected to establish a drift-corrected heading and hold it instead of chasing the indicator.

error_modes.label: Programming of preplanned turning points and mission parameters

texts.0: SP, due to incomplete preflight preparation, did not program all preplanned turning points and the parameters necessary for mission execution into the GPS. Waypoints were missing or loaded out of sequence, and the displayed route did not match the briefed plan. The IP had to stop the sequence and rebuild the flight plan for the mission to continue.
texts.1: SP, due to rushed data entry on the ground, loaded the turning points with errors that surfaced only after engine start. The flight plan was corrected at the limit of the available time and only after the IP pointed out the discrepancies. SP did not verify the entries against the mission planning material.
texts.2: SP, due to omitting the readback of entered coordinates, loaded one turning point incorrectly. SP found the error during the self-check of the route legs and corrected it before taxi without IP involvement. Leg headings and total distance were then verified against the plan.
texts.3: SP programmed all preplanned turning points and the required parameters accurately and in the correct sequence. Each entry was verified against the planning material by leg course and distance. The loaded route matched the briefed plan with no further correction.
texts.4: SP loaded the complete route into the GPS quickly and without a single entry error. Verification was systematic, covering waypoint identifiers, leg courses, distances and total route length. The programmed plan was ready well before it was needed.
texts.marginal: SP produced a correct GPS flight plan but needed several attempts and more time than expected to complete the entries. Verification was performed once and covered distances but not leg courses. SP is expected to build a repeatable entry and check routine so that programming is complete and verified within normal planning time.

error_modes.label: Crosscheck of GPS data with other available navaids and map

texts.0: SP, due to a lapse in monitoring and crosschecking, accepted the GPS picture without comparing it with the VOR-DME/TACAN indications and the map. A gross position error went unrecognized and the aircraft was flown well off the planned route, holding a heading error beyond 10 degrees toward a wrong turning point. The IP had to intervene to re-establish the correct navigation.
texts.1: SP, due to weak monitoring of the other available navaids, made only one comparison of GPS data with the TACAN and the map during the whole leg. The mismatch was identified at the limit of usable time and only after the IP prompted the crosscheck. The route was regained, but the turning point was reached with a significant track offset.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on the GPS display, delayed the comparison with the TACAN and the map until midway through the leg. SP then detected the disagreement, resolved it against visual checkpoints and corrected a heading error of less than 10 degrees on its own initiative. The plan was maintained without IP input.
texts.3: SP crosschecked GPS data with the available navaids and the map on every leg. Position, bearing and distance were compared and agreed, and each small discrepancy was resolved immediately. Navigation stayed accurate with heading within 5 degrees of the computed course.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous and disciplined comparison of GPS information with TACAN, DME and visual map references. Each turning point was confirmed by at least two independent sources before the turn was started. No discrepancy was allowed to develop into a navigation error.
texts.marginal: SP performed the required crosscheck with the other navaids, but the comparison was routinely made after the turn rather than before it. The habit left little margin to catch a position error in time. SP is expected to complete the navaid and map comparison prior to each turning point, so that GPS data is confirmed rather than assumed.

error_modes.label: Knowledge and efficient use of GPS capabilities

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the GPS pages and functions, did not use the capabilities required by the mission. Basic operations such as direct-to routing, waypoint sequencing and data retrieval were attempted incorrectly or abandoned. The IP had to operate the equipment for the navigation task to be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to shallow familiarity with the menu structure, needed several attempts to reach the required GPS functions. The correct page was found only after the IP described the sequence. Navigation continued, but the delay disturbed the timing of the following leg.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation with a less frequently used GPS function, initially selected the wrong page. SP recognized the error, worked back through the menu and completed the intended operation in good time and without assistance. Mission timing was preserved.
texts.3: SP demonstrated good knowledge of the GPS and used its capabilities correctly and efficiently. Page selection, direct-to routing and data extraction were performed without hesitation. The equipment was used as a navigation aid at the pace the mission required.
texts.4: SP used the full range of GPS capabilities fluently and to the advantage of the mission. Functions were selected with no search time, including those beyond routine use. The equipment was handled as a well-understood tool rather than as an additional task.
texts.marginal: SP used the GPS correctly for routine functions but was noticeably slower whenever a less common capability was required. Knowledge was adequate without being consolidated across the full menu structure. SP is expected to practice the complete set of GPS functions so that all capabilities are available at operational speed.

error_modes.label: Airborne GPS workload versus aircraft control priority

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on a single GPS entry problem, allowed the equipment task to capture the entire scan while airborne. Aircraft control and lookout lapsed, altitude departed by more than 300 feet and the aircraft continued past the turning point. The IP had to take over the navigation task to restore the flight profile.
texts.1: SP, due to fixation on the GPS while airborne, did not divide attention between the equipment and aircraft control. Altitude and heading deviations reached the limits of tolerance and were corrected only after the IP called for a return to the instruments. SP did not break the fixation without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an extended head-down period spent correcting a waypoint, briefly lost the priority of aircraft control. SP recognized the fixation, returned to the scan and corrected deviations that had stayed between the code 3 and code 1 zones. The GPS entry was then completed without further loss of control priority.
texts.3: SP kept the GPS workload subordinate to flying the aircraft. Head-down periods were short and deliberately broken by returns to the scan, so all parameters remained within the tighter limits. Equipment tasks were placed at points in the leg where workload allowed them.
texts.4: SP managed the airborne GPS workload with clear task prioritization. Entries were split into short blocks, each separated by a full instrument and outside scan, and no parameter moved appreciably. Aircraft control was never traded for equipment management.
texts.marginal: SP maintained control priority overall, but one unexpected GPS response held SP's attention longer than briefed before the scan was resumed. Standards were kept, although the margin narrowed during that period. SP is expected to set a fixed limit on head-down time and return to the scan before working the problem further.

error_modes.label: Independent navigation picture versus reliance on GPS

texts.0: SP, due to over-reliance on the GPS, navigated solely by the moving map and abandoned map reading and dead reckoning. When the displayed information did not match the ground picture, SP had no independent means of fixing position and continued toward a wrong feature. The IP had to intervene to re-establish orientation and regain the planned route.
texts.1: SP, due to accepting the GPS as the only navigation reference, could not confirm position by ground features when required. The independent check was produced only after the IP directed it and after a delay that left the aircraft at the limit of the planned track. SP's confidence in the display was not supported by verification.
texts.2: SP, due to a preference for the GPS display, initially disregarded the visual checkpoints of the leg. SP recognized the omission, re-established the ground picture against the map and confirmed position independently in good time. Navigation continued on plan without IP input.
texts.3: SP used the GPS as one navigation source among several and kept an independent picture from map reading and timing. Position was confirmed by ground features at each checkpoint. Awareness of the route did not depend on the equipment.
texts.4: SP integrated GPS information with map reading, timing and visual features so that each source reinforced the others. SP could state position, time and distance to the next turning point at any moment without reference to the display. Navigation would have continued unaffected had the equipment failed.
texts.marginal: SP kept an independent navigation picture but turned to the GPS first whenever position was in question. Map and timing checks were carried out, though only to confirm what the display had already shown. SP is expected to establish position from the ground picture first and use the GPS to verify it.

error_modes.label: GPS as advisory source versus primary source: VOR and DME raw data

texts.0: SP, due to using the GPS as a primary source of navigation instead of an advisory one, did not tune, identify or monitor the VOR and DME for the leg. The displayed course was followed with no raw data backup, the aircraft was flown off the planned track with a heading error beyond 10 degrees and the divergence went unrecognized. The IP had to intervene and re-establish the navigation on the radial and the DME distance.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the GPS as the primary navigation reference, tuned the VOR and DME only after being directed to and never identified the station by its ident. Raw data entered the crosscheck at the limit of usable time, with the track error already about 10 degrees off the computed course. Repeated verbal prompting was needed before the GPS course was verified against the radial.
texts.2: SP, due to working the GPS first and the navaids second, delayed tuning and identifying the VOR and DME for the leg. SP recognized that the advisory role of the equipment requires raw data backup, set the navaids up and confirmed the course while keeping the heading error under 10 degrees. The correction was made in good time and without IP input.
texts.3: SP used the GPS in its advisory role and kept the VOR and DME tuned, identified and inside the crosscheck. The GPS course was treated as confirmation of the raw data rather than as a replacement for it, and heading was held within 5 degrees of the computed course. Navaid skills were exercised on every leg of the route.
texts.4: SP navigated on VOR and DME raw data throughout and used the GPS only as an advisory overlay. Each station was tuned and identified before it was needed and the two pictures agreed at every checkpoint. Track and heading were held with negligible deviation and the priority between the sources was never inverted.
texts.marginal: SP kept the VOR and DME tuned and navigation remained within standards, but every course decision was taken from the GPS first and the raw data was only glanced at afterwards. The advisory source was in practice leading the navigation. SP is expected to fly the leg on raw data and use the GPS to confirm it, so that VOR and DME skills continue to be developed.

error_modes.label: Groundspeed check for the effects of wind

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the groundspeed check after level off, never determined the effects of the winds on the route. Neither the GPS groundspeed nor the DME change over one minute was used, so the planned drift correction and ETAs were carried unchanged. The aircraft reached the area of the turning point with a heading error beyond 10 degrees and a timing error the IP had to correct.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the groundspeed check until late in the leg, flew on wind values that no longer matched the actual conditions. The GPS groundspeed was read only after the IP prompted it and the revised drift correction was applied at the limit of tolerance, with the heading error about 10 degrees. Timing to the turning point had already slipped noticeably.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed groundspeed check, initially held the planned heading against outdated wind data. SP then read groundspeed from the GPS, compared it with the planned figure and revised the drift correction on its own initiative, keeping the heading error under 10 degrees. The updated ETA was established before the turning point.
texts.3: SP accomplished a groundspeed check shortly after level off from the GPS readout and confirmed it with the DME change over one minute. The wind effect was quantified and the drift correction applied, holding heading within 5 degrees of the computed course. ETAs were updated for the remaining legs.
texts.4: SP checked groundspeed at level off and rechecked it on each leg, so the wind effect was known at all times. Drift correction and ETAs were revised before any error could develop and the timing method was used to cross-confirm the GPS figure. Track and timing were maintained with negligible deviation.
texts.marginal: SP performed the groundspeed check, but only once at the start of the route and never revised it as the wind changed along the legs. Navigation stayed within standards while the timing error grew steadily toward the end. SP is expected to repeat the groundspeed check on each leg so that the wind correction stays representative.

error_modes.label: Fuel prediction at future points from actual fuel flow versus planned fuel

texts.0: SP, due to never combining groundspeed with the actual fuel flow on the EID, did not predict fuel at the future points of the route. Changes to the planned routing, altitude and winds were not recognized as drivers of a fuel difference and planned figures were quoted as if they were actual. The IP had to compute the fuel state and impose a change to the plan.
texts.1: SP, due to comparing planned against actual fuel only once, did not notice that a delay and an off-plan altitude had shifted the consumption. The discrepancy was raised only after the IP asked for the fuel at the next turning point and the recomputation came at the limit of usable time. The route was continued on a fuel picture that had not been updated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on the navigation display, initially skipped the fuel check at the first turning point. SP recognized the omission, took the actual fuel flow from the EID with the GPS groundspeed and rebuilt the prediction for the remaining points in good time. No IP input was required and the plan remained valid.
texts.3: SP predicted fuel at the future points of the route from groundspeed and the actual fuel flow shown on the EID. Planned, updated and actual figures were compared at each turning point and the small differences were explained by the winds and the flown altitude. The fuel picture stayed consistent with the mission plan.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuously updated fuel prediction, revising it whenever routing, altitude, wind or temperature departed from the plan. Each turning point was reached with the actual figure already compared against the planned and updated values. The fuel state was known at all times without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP compared planned and actual fuel at the required points, but the updated prediction was recomputed only when the difference had already become obvious. The figures stayed inside the mission plan while the checks lagged the changes that caused them. SP is expected to revise the fuel prediction as soon as routing, altitude or winds differ from the plan, not after the difference has grown.

error_modes.label: Task prioritization and in-flight checks during the busiest portions of the sortie

texts.0: SP, due to poor task prioritization in the busiest portions of the sortie, worked the GPS through the clearance and level off sequence and omitted the required in-flight checks. Without the cues of the local training environment no memory aid was used and the omission was never detected by SP. The IP had to stop the equipment work and direct the checks before the route could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to loading GPS tasks into the phase between the clearance call and level off, ran the in-flight checks late and incompletely. The missing items were covered only after the IP listed them and the flight parameters were held at the limit of tolerance while SP caught up. No memory aid was in place to protect the checks.
texts.2: SP, due to starting a GPS entry sequence during the level off, delayed the in-flight check beyond its normal point. SP recognized the conflict, stopped the entries, completed the check and returned to the equipment afterwards without IP involvement. The parameters were kept inside the intermediate band throughout.
texts.3: SP prioritized the tasks correctly through the busy portions of the sortie and completed the required in-flight checks at their proper points. GPS work was deferred to the quiet parts of the leg and the aircraft was flown within 150 feet and 5 degrees while the checks were made. Nothing was omitted from the sequence.
texts.4: SP scheduled all GPS work around the required checks and used memory aids to protect them away from the local training environment. Every in-flight check was completed at its point with the aircraft held on parameters. Workload through the clearance, level off and descent phases was distributed so that no task competed with another.
texts.marginal: SP completed the required in-flight checks and kept the aircraft on parameters, but each check was started only when the GPS work happened to allow it. The order of tasks depended on the equipment rather than on the phase of the sortie. SP is expected to fix the checks to their points and fit the GPS work around them, especially between the clearance call and level off.

error_modes.label: Emergency airfield awareness and use of the GPS nearest function

texts.0: SP, due to never using the GPS nearest function or the map for this purpose, could not identify a suitable emergency airfield at any point of the route. No what if drill was carried out and, when questioned, SP had no bearing, distance or fuel figure to any recovery field. The IP had to establish the diversion picture for the sortie to continue.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving emergency airfield awareness to the planning stage only, did not refresh it as the route progressed. A nearest field was produced only after the IP asked for it and the data was assembled at the limit of usable time. The what if drill was carried out under direction rather than on SP initiative.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on the leg navigation, initially let the emergency airfield picture lapse. SP recognized the omission, used the GPS nearest function to identify a suitable field and confirmed bearing, distance and fuel required in good time. The drill was completed without IP input.
texts.3: SP identified suitable emergency airfields periodically along the route and used the GPS nearest function to support the choice. Bearing, distance and fuel required were available on request on each leg. Decision making was practiced with what if drills as the route progressed.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous diversion picture, naming the nearest suitable field with its bearing, distance and fuel at any moment of the route. The GPS nearest function was used to confirm a decision SP had already reasoned through from the map. What if drills were run without prompting on every leg.
texts.marginal: SP identified emergency airfields when asked and the data given was correct, but the check was repeated only at the turning points and not as the route moved away from them. The diversion picture was accurate rather than current. SP is expected to refresh the nearest suitable field continuously along the leg, not only at the planned points.

error_modes.label: Enroute descent start down point computed from GPS distance to go

texts.0: SP, due to not computing the start down point from the 2 to 1 ratio plus 10 miles, requested the descent with no distance reference taken from the GPS or the DME. The descent was started well past the required point, the planned gradient could not be flown and the altitude at the following fix was beyond 300 feet from the plan. The IP had to take over the descent planning to recover the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a late computation of the desired start down point, requested the descent only after the IP pointed at the distance to go. The gradient then had to be steepened well past 5 degrees and airspeed was held at the limit of tolerance through the descent. The planned altitude was regained only close to the fix.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial error in the 2 to 1 computation, planned the start down point without the extra 10 miles for the approach. SP rechecked the figure against the GPS distance to go, corrected the request in good time and flew the descent close to the planned gradient. Altitude and airspeed stayed inside the intermediate band.
texts.3: SP computed the desired start down point using the 2 to 1 ratio plus 10 miles and confirmed it against the GPS distance to go. The descent was requested to match the desired profile and the gradient was held near 5 degrees. Altitude at the following fix was within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots of the plan.
texts.4: SP had the start down point computed and cross-confirmed well before it was needed and requested the descent to match the desired profile exactly. Distance to go was monitored throughout, so the gradient never had to be reworked. Altitude and airspeed through the descent showed negligible deviation from the plan.
texts.marginal: SP computed the start down point correctly and flew the descent within standards, but the request was made only when the distance to go had almost run out. Any delay in the clearance would have forced a gradient steeper than planned. SP is expected to compute and request the descent early enough to keep the planned 5 degree gradient available.

error_modes.label: Temporary disorientation: climb to MSA until positive position is regained
error_modes.source: technique:8.20.3 MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE (MSA), EMERGENCY ROUTE ABORT ALTITUDE (ERAA) AND ROUTE ABORTS

texts.0: SP, due to temporary disorientation with regard to navigation, continued at the flown altitude instead of climbing to the MSA of the leg and kept searching the GPS display for a fix. Position was never positively regained and the aircraft was flown on with the route error beyond 10 degrees of heading. The IP had to intervene, initiate the climb and re-establish the position with the map and the navaids.
texts.1: SP, due to losing the position picture on the leg, delayed the climb to MSA and continued at low level while working the equipment. The climb was started only after the IP directed it and position was regained at the limit of usable time, with an altitude excursion of about 300 feet during the recovery. The distraction of low altitude flight was not recognized as a factor.
texts.2: SP, due to a temporary loss of the position picture, initially pressed on with the map and the GPS at the flown altitude. SP recognized the disorientation, climbed toward the MSA of the leg and regained a positive fix from the navaids in good time, holding the intermediate deviation bands throughout. No IP input was required.
texts.3: SP recognized the doubt about position immediately and climbed to the MSA of the leg while re-establishing the fix with the map, the GPS and the navaids. Altitude was held within 150 feet of the MSA during the recovery and the route was rejoined once position was positive. The sequence of climb first and navigate second was followed.
texts.4: SP never allowed the position picture to lapse and, at the first ambiguity, climbed at once toward the MSA with the fix re-established from independent sources before the climb was complete. Aircraft control through the climb showed negligible deviation. The MSA of each leg and the ERAA of the route were available from memory at any moment.
texts.marginal: SP recovered the position within standards, but the climb toward the MSA was started only after two attempts to resolve the doubt on the GPS. The habit places the equipment ahead of terrain clearance when position is uncertain. SP is expected to climb to the MSA first and regain the fix afterwards, since low altitude flight increases distraction and complicates the recovery.
